NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 | Student research review • 2
Scientific notice and scope of use
This document is a student literature review and an information-system design proposal. It does not 
represent an official NASA position, certify any spacecraft material or system, or provide operational 
fire-suppression instructions for a crewed vehicle. In an actual emergency, the governing instructions 
are the vehicle-specific approved emergency procedures and directions from the crew and responsible 
operator. The discussion of heat transfer, flow, and flame sensitivity is scientific interpretation 
bounded by the experiments cited here.
The reference cut-off date for the original review is 14 November 2026. Program pages and challenge 
requirements may change after that date. The original review was prepared before the additional raw 
data files discussed in the appended English update and data-analysis appendix were uploaded. The 
update note explicitly identifies which earlier statements have been superseded and which data 
remain unavailable.
Abstract
This review examines how ignition, flame spread, extinction, soot formation, and smoke-aerosol 
transport change when buoyancy is weakened, as in the microgravity environment of the 
International Space Station (ISS), or reduced to approximately one-sixth of Earth gravity on the lunar 
surface. It critically reviews NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations and relevant NASA 
standards and technical guidance, including SPICE, BASS/BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SoFIE, FM², FLEX/FLEX-2, 
CFI, SAME/SAME-R, MPASS, and ACME. The review distinguishes reported observations from physical 
interpretation and proposed engineering concepts. It corrects several overgeneralizations in the 
preliminary draft: flame shape and extinction are condition-dependent; low airflow does not 
universally guarantee extinction; FM² is described in NASA sources as a planned lunar investigation 
supported by terrestrial reduced-gravity tests; and SPICE point counts differ between a peer-reviewed 
paper and a conference abstract.
The paper proposes the Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas (LFAEA), a traceable, AI-assisted 
dashboard that organizes experiment metadata, compares only compatible conditions, exposes 
uncertainty, and supports evidence-based interpretation for lunar and deep-space habitat safety. It is a 
student research prototype, not a NASA-approved fire-safety system.
Keywords: microgravity combustion; lunar gravity; heat and mass transfer; smoke point; soot; smoke 
aerosols; spacecraft fire safety; NASA PSI; BASS-II; SPICE; SAFFIRE; SoFIE; FM²; MPASS.

1. Introduction and spacecraft fire-safety context
Fire is a compound hazard aboard crewed spacecraft. The risk is not limited to flame or direct heat: 
combustion products may include irritating or toxic gases, visibility may be lost, filters and equipment 
may be contaminated, and a compartment may need to be isolated or evacuated. Escape options in a 
sealed vehicle are more constrained than in terrestrial buildings. The cabin atmosphere is a limited 
engineered system requiring careful control of oxygen, pressure, humidity, and contaminant removal. 
NASA technical guidance describes fire protection as an integrated strategy involving material 
selection, detection, suppression, crew response, and post-event cleanup [20].
The space environment differs from a terrestrial laboratory not simply because gravity is absent. 
Gravity drives buoyancy-induced natural convection when hot and cold gases have different densities. 
On Earth, hot gases rise, entrain surrounding air, and often create an upward-stretched flame. In 
microgravity this mechanism is greatly weakened, increasing the relative importance of molecular 
diffusion, thermal conduction, radiation, and forced ventilation. The direction and speed of ventilation 
can therefore strongly affect oxygen supply and product removal. This does not mean that every flame 
becomes a perfect sphere: flame shape also depends on geometry, burner placement, sample 
orientation, and imposed flow.
NASA PSI is important because it aggregates experimental data from different investigations and 
missions, allowing researchers to revisit evidence rather than relying only on conclusions in published 
summaries. The repository spans solid-material combustion, droplet burning, diffusion flames, and 
smoke aerosols. Data and documentation completeness vary among investigations [6]. A responsible 
information system must therefore distinguish a PSI investigation record, a raw data file, a processed 
dataset, an engineering report, and a peer-reviewed publication as different evidence layers.
These questions become increasingly relevant for long-duration missions, return to the Moon, and 
farther exploration. A lunar habitat may contain a pressurized and composition-controlled internal 
atmosphere, while the external surface environment is near-vacuum, thermally extreme, and dusty. 
Fire behavior inside a habitat cannot be inferred directly from the external lunar environment. The 
pressurized internal atmosphere is the setting for ignition and sustained combustion; external dust, 
temperature, radiation, and surface conditions may affect materials and systems but are separate 
boundary conditions.
The central premise of this review is that no single number or experiment represents “fire safety in 
space.” Each result must remain linked to its experimental context, and the validity of comparison 
with another environment must be assessed explicitly.

2. Research problem, questions, objectives, and scope
The research problem is the fragmentation of evidence on material combustion in microgravity and 
the variation in measurement and documentation methods across investigations. Some reports record 
air velocity, pressure, and oxygen concentration; others focus on fuel type or flame shape; still others 
measure smoke and particle properties. Combining these results without unit harmonization or 
verification of test conditions can produce engineering conclusions that exceed the data, such as a 
universal extinction threshold or a universal particle-size distribution for all spacecraft materials.
The problem becomes more visible when results from the ISS are transferred to a lunar facility. Lunar 
gravity may modify natural convection without eliminating it, and a lunar habitat may have a 
different forced-ventilation pattern, pressure, and gas composition. There are also scale gaps between 
small laboratory flames and large fires, and a diagnostic gap between measurements of flame behavior 
and the actual response of smoke detectors.
2.1 Primary research question
How can NASA PSI findings on combustion, soot, and smoke aerosols in microgravity and partial-
gravity environments be harmonized into a traceable comparative framework that supports 
understanding of fire risk in crewed spacecraft and lunar habitats, without exceeding the evidence or 
presenting unvalidated operational predictions?
2.2 Sub-questions
1.
Which physical variables explain differences among flames in 1g, microgravity, and 1/6g 
environments?
2.
What does NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 specifically measure, and what cannot be inferred from it?
3.
What experimental results are documented for SPICE, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SoFIE, FM², FLEX/CFI, 
SAME/MPASS, and ACME?
4.
How do burner geometry, coflow speed, and fuel affect the smoke point?
5.
How do smoke aerosols evolve, and what are the limits of using aerosol moments and optical-
scattering measurements?
6.
What metadata and calibration records are required to reproduce mass-flow-controller (MFC) 
conversions?
7.
How can an AI-assisted dashboard support search, comparison, and interpretation while exposing 
evidence strength and provenance?
2.3 Objectives

Prepare a critical review of primary sources, official reports, and peer-reviewed papers on space 
combustion investigations.

Audit numerical claims, equations, and experiment names from the preliminary draft, classifying 
each as documented, conditional, or unverified.

Explain the physical and chemical mechanisms associated with heat transfer, mass transfer, flow, 
ignition, extinction, and soot formation.

Propose a standardized data schema linking each result to its conditions, instruments, calibration, 
and source file.

Design a demonstrable student project called the Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas in alignment 
with the “Flame in Freefall” challenge.
2.4 Testable hypotheses
Hypothesis 1: At fixed fuel, gas composition, pressure, and geometry, reducing or removing buoyancy 
changes heat- and mass-transfer distributions around the reaction zone, but the direction of the effect

surface temperature, and extinction limits in a controlled matrix.
Hypothesis 2: Forced-flow speed does not affect all flame metrics linearly or in a single direction. It 
may increase oxygen supply and reaction rate while reducing local residence time for volatile fuel and 
soot precursors. The net effect depends on the experiment. Measurements should include flame length, 
fuel flow, smoke threshold, and particle distributions.
Hypothesis 3: Smoke-detector performance cannot be evaluated from particle number alone. It also 
depends on size distribution, morphology, refractive index, electrical properties, transport to the 
detector, and alarm threshold. Tests should compare detector response to aerosol samples with 
documented morphology and record arrival time and false-alarm rates.
2.5 Scope and limitations
The original review did not perform a complete reanalysis of all raw datasets from NASA PSI, and it 
did not conduct new CFD simulations or material tests. Some data files were not available at the time. 
Later uploads enabled a targeted descriptive analysis of selected SPICE, PSI-159, and PSI-142 files, 
documented in the appended data-analysis appendix. This remains a partial analysis, not a complete 
reprocessing of all PSI investigations. Any proposed prediction in the dashboard is an exploratory 
classification or visualization tool, not a control instrument or safety certification.
3. Review methodology and evidence-strength classification
The review uses a structured descriptive-analytical method. Investigations were identified through 
NASA PSI and the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), followed by relevant NASA Science and 
NASA Glenn pages and, where available, peer-reviewed papers and DOI records. NASA reports and 
documents authored by experiment investigators were prioritized for apparatus configuration, 
operation, and results. Secondary sources were retained only where they help explain context or 
history; they were not used to validate a numerical result absent from a primary source.
Search terms combined investigation names, PSI identifiers, and technical expressions such as 
microgravity combustion, flame extinction, smoke point, coflow burner, smoke aerosol, lunar 
flammability, SoFIE, FM2, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, FLEX, CFI, SAME-R, MPASS, and NASA-STD-6001. Search-
engine summaries were not treated as scientific data. Available pages were opened, document text was 
reviewed, and permanent URLs or DOI records were retained when possible.
3.1 Inclusion criteria

The source is issued by NASA, NTRS, PSI, a scientific journal, or a relevant technical conference 
with a DOI or verifiable publication record.

It directly concerns material combustion, flames, fuel droplets, soot, smoke aerosols, or spacecraft 
fire protection.

It provides data or an experimental description linked to a clear context such as fuel, gravity 
environment, flow, oxygen concentration, or diagnostic instrument.

The source has an identifiable title and author or responsible organization, with date, report 
number, or DOI where available.
3.2 Exclusion and caution criteria

Numerical claims without an identifiable primary source were excluded.

Conference and peer-reviewed results were not merged when counts, fits, or definitions differed.

MFC voltages were not converted to flow rates without channel definition, gas identity, calibration 
curve, and reference conditions.

4. Physical foundations: heat transfer, mass transfer, and buoyancy
Combustion is a coupled process involving chemical reaction, fluid motion, heat transfer, and mass 
transfer. A flame persists when heat released by chemical reaction is sufficient to offset heat losses and 
maintain the reactants within a reactive temperature and composition range. The relative importance 
of transport mechanisms changes when buoyancy is weakened, but none of the mechanisms should be 
assumed to disappear completely.
4.1 Buoyancy and natural convection
In terrestrial gravity, heating reduces gas density and produces buoyant motion. This drives a natural-
convection plume, entrains surrounding oxidizer, and carries hot products away. In microgravity, the 
buoyancy-driven acceleration is greatly reduced, so molecular diffusion and imposed ventilation 
become more important. However, “microgravity” aboard the ISS does not mean that all accelerations 
vanish: vehicle disturbances, crew activity, equipment motion, and residual accelerations remain. 
Lunar gravity is a steady partial-gravity environment of roughly one-sixth Earth gravity, not 
microgravity.
4.2 Molecular diffusion and forced ventilation
Molecular diffusion transports species down concentration gradients. Forced ventilation transports 
species and heat through an imposed flow field. In the absence of strong buoyancy, a modest forced 
flow can become important because it changes oxygen delivery, fuel-vapor transport, residence time, 
and product removal. The effect is not necessarily monotonic: increased flow may enhance oxidation 
by supplying oxygen, cool or stretch a flame, displace the reaction zone, or reduce the time available 
for soot growth.
4.3 Conduction and radiation
Heat is transferred by conduction within the fuel, gas, and supporting structures, and by radiation 
through the surrounding space. In some terrestrial flames, convection carries a substantial fraction of 
thermal energy; in microgravity, radiation and conduction may become more prominent in the energy

A flame may become more symmetric around a fuel source when the vertical buoyancy gradient is

For a flame-spread question, Gr and Ra help assess natural-convection effects, Pe indicates the 
importance of imposed flow relative to diffusion, and Da connects flow/residence time with chemistry. 
These groups alone do not supply an ignition limit, flame-spread speed, or extinction threshold. They 
must be connected to observations such as flame length over time, surface temperature, or local 
oxygen concentration.
6. Diffusion flames, ignition limits, and extinction
A diffusion flame is one in which the reaction zone forms where fuel and oxidizer meet and mix by 
transport, rather than from a premixed uniform reactant mixture. This structure occurs in burning 
solids, evaporating droplets, and gaseous jet burners. Flame propagation and stabilization depend on 
the balance between heat and mass transfer and chemical reaction rates. Chemistry depends on local 
temperature and composition; heat feedback depends on products, transport, geometry, and losses.
6.1 Ignition and flame spread over solids
For a solid material, ignition generally begins when the surface is heated enough to decompose or 
release combustible vapors. Those vapors mix with oxygen and reach conditions where a self-
sustaining reaction can occur. The flame may feed heat back to adjacent material through hot gases, 
radiation, and conduction within the solid. If the feedback is sufficient to heat the next region and 
generate more fuel vapor, a flame front may spread. Sample thickness, orientation, preheating, 
thermal properties, oxygen concentration, and ventilation all affect the process.
In microgravity, heat-transfer paths and oxygen distribution change, but it is not valid to assume that 
flame spread is always faster or always slower. Reduced natural convection may reduce convective 
cooling at a surface, while also reducing oxygen delivery to the reaction zone. Forced flow may 
enhance reaction, remove heat, or shift the flame location. The result is set by the combined balance, 
which is why BASS/BASS-II results must remain tied to their sample and flow conditions.
6.2 Ignition, sustainability, and spread are different limits
Flammability limits are not fixed material constants independent of pressure, temperature, geometry, 
and flow. A sample may ignite under one oxygen concentration or flow condition and fail under 
another. It is useful to distinguish: (i) ignition, the condition for initiating reaction; (ii) flame 
sustainability, the condition that permits the flame to persist after ignition; and (iii) flame spread, the 
condition that allows the flame front to move to adjacent material. These limits are not 
interchangeable. A local point may ignite and then extinguish without spread, or a local flame may 
persist without propagating along the sample.

6.3 Extinction mechanisms
Extinction may occur when energy losses exceed chemical heat release, when one reactant becomes 
insufficient, or when residence time becomes too short to sustain reaction. Increased flow can cause 
flame lift-off or blowoff in some configurations, but the threshold depends on scale, flame shape, fuel 
properties, and apparatus. A small flame may also be extinguished by radiative or conductive losses 
under particular conditions. No universal rule states that turning off airflow will extinguish every fire; 
airflow may also be part of the system that removes heat and products, and stopping it can alter 
oxygen distribution in a complex way.
A velocity that causes blowoff in a small gaseous jet flame is not automatically equivalent to a velocity 
that extinguishes a flame spreading over a solid sample. Increased speed may increase convective heat 
transfer, oxygen transport, or reduce residence time; the net result is configuration-dependent. 
Numerical values in experiment reports must therefore remain linked to fuel, sample geometry, 
pressure, oxygen composition, and measurement location.
These mechanisms must not be converted into operational advice for crew response. Changing 
ventilation or cabin gas composition is a safety-critical decision controlled by certified vehicle 
procedures and system logic. This review explains the physics of published investigations; it is not a 
substitute for an emergency response procedure. NASA’s fire-protection technical brief describes an 
integrated response including detection, warning, compartment ventilation logic, crew protection, and 
system isolation [20].
7. Regulatory framework: reading NASA-STD-6001B
NASA-STD-6001, “Flammability, Odor, Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures 
for Materials in Environments That Support Combustion,” defines requirements for evaluating, testing, 
and selecting materials for spacecraft and ground-support equipment. The NASA standards page lists 
Version B, Change 3, dated 9 June 2025, as active at the reference cut-off date [1]. It covers 
flammability, offgassing, and compatibility; it is not merely a single flame-spread test. Any formal use 
should cite the full designation, version, and change date.
7.1 Test 1: upward flame propagation / vertical flammability
Test 1 is a vertical upward flame-propagation test intended to assess whether a sample self-
extinguishes and whether flaming debris can ignite adjacent material. The standard describes multiple 
specimens with defined dimensions, mounted vertically and ignited from below. Acceptance criteria 
include limits on flame propagation and prevention of ignition of other specimens by falling flaming 
particles [1]. The complete official standard and its controlled procedures must be consulted for exact 
dimensions, preparation, and acceptance details.
7.2 What the test does and does not demonstrate
The purpose is to screen materials under a specified test environment and upward-flame 
configuration. The result is valuable because it enables repeatable comparison among materials and 
batches. However, a 1g upward-flame test does not alone cover every combination of reduced gravity, 
forced ventilation, oxygen fraction, pressure, geometry, or sample orientation that may occur in a 
mission habitat. It is not correct to call the standard irrelevant: it is an important baseline for material 
risk reduction. It is also not correct to treat it as a complete substitute for mission-specific evaluation 
when the gravity and flow conditions are different.
The defensible interpretation is that NASA-STD-6001B provides a standardized material screening 
framework within its test conditions. Additional mission-specific testing or analysis may be needed to

8.1 Investigation identifiers and relationships
A PSI identifier, a mission payload name, a Cygnus flight number, and a paper DOI are not 
interchangeable. One investigation may have multiple repository records or publications, and a 
publication may combine flight and ground data. The proposed system should maintain a crosswalk 
table linking investigation_id, mission_name, payload, paper_doi, and dataset_version without 
converting one identifier into another. This preserves traceability when a project is renamed or 
reflown.
8.2 Data layers within a repository record
Repository content should be classified as raw data, processed data, engineering documentation, or 
scientific publication. Raw data require unit definitions, calibration, and decoding. Processed data may 
have undergone filters or corrections. Engineering reports describe hardware and operations but may 
not be peer-reviewed. A paper presents selected analyses and may not publish every measurement. 
The dashboard should display file type before allowing a user to treat a figure or summary as raw 
data.

8.3 Relationships across investigations
Some investigations share scientific questions but use different measurement approaches. SPICE can 
examine the onset of visible soot in a gaseous flame; SAME examines aerosols from overheated 
spacecraft materials, including cases without an established flame; BASS-II examines burning and 
flame spread over solid samples. These topics connect at the system-design level but should not be 
collapsed into a single variable. A knowledge graph should use explicit relationship types such as “uses 
related material,” “measures a combustion product,” “uses a shared platform,” or “cites the same 
report,” rather than a generic arrow that implies scientific equivalence.
9. SPICE and smoke-point behavior in microgravity
The Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) examined smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant 
round-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air aboard the ISS. The smoke point is a useful indicator of a 
fuel’s tendency to produce visible soot in a specified burner configuration. Soot affects radiative heat 
transfer and is relevant to air quality and smoke-detector design, but smoke point alone is not a soot 
mass-generation rate, particle count, or cabin smoke concentration [7-9].
9.1 Smoke-point definition and test context
The smoke point is the condition or luminous flame length at which visible soot emission begins, 
according to the measurement protocol used. It is a comparative property for a specified fuel, burner, 
and flow configuration. The burner type and diameter, fuel composition, coflow speed, and optical 
criterion must accompany each reported value.
9.2 Published counts and fit
The peer-reviewed Fire Safety Journal article reports 55 smoke points for nonbuoyant coflowing 
flames, with burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities between 5.4 and 65 cm/s. 
It gives an empirical correlation of the form:

This is an empirical fit for the fuels, geometries, and conditions studied; it is not a universal law for 
every flame or fuel. It should not be applied directly to solid fuels, lunar gravity, or a closed habitat 
without validation. A separate conference paper reports 52 smoke points and a different reported fit 
[7, 8].
9.3 Why 55 and 52 must remain separate
The peer-reviewed article reports 55 points, while the conference proceedings report 52. The sources 
available for this review do not establish in sufficient detail whether the difference arose from a 
preliminary dataset, acceptance criteria, removed measurements, or a later analysis update. The 
figures must not be combined or presented as a single count of 107. In a database, each count should 
be stored with publication_id, version, and definition_of_valid_point.
9.4 Burner diameter, coflow, and interpretation
Burner geometry affects velocity distribution, fuel delivery, and the distance over which gases move 
before reacting. Smaller diameters alter area-to-flow relationships and characteristic diffusion scales. 
Coflow velocity affects residence time, aerodynamic strain, and oxygen supply. A rise in smoke-point 
luminous length with coflow in a defined dataset is not necessarily inconsistent with shorter local 
residence time for some species: the smoke-point measurement is the fuel-flow condition at visible soot

reported separately.
9.5 Threshold Soot Index and design implications
Some combustion literature uses a soot tendency index to compare fuels, but its equation, units, and 
calibration must come from the specific source. Numerical pseudo-Threshold Soot Index values in the 
preliminary draft were not fully verified here and are therefore not presented as confirmed results. 
The dashboard should store such an index only when the definition and calculation method are 
documented. A relative fuel-ranking index is not equivalent to soot mass rate or airborne particle 
concentration.
SPICE demonstrates that soot-related measurements can be conducted in microgravity and that burner 
geometry and coflow matter for the smoke point. It does not provide a complete smoke-detector design 
or represent every spacecraft material. Its strongest value for LFAEA is a traceable fuel-burner-flow-
output record, with the original fit shown only in the conditions where it was derived.
10. Solid-material combustion: BASS and BASS-II
The Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) and BASS-II investigations studied ignition, burning, and 
suppression of solid materials in microgravity. NASA reports describe samples with different shapes 
and thicknesses, including polymer slabs and other sample forms, tested in a small flow duct that 
allows air speed to be varied around the specimen [10, 11].
10.1 Flow range and observed sensitivity
The reviewed BASS-II materials describe a test system with airflow reaching approximately 53 cm/s 
and a pronounced flame response in the low-flow range of 0-5 cm/s. They also report that a faint blue 
flame could persist at below 1 cm/s in some test conditions. These observations show that very weak 
air currents can remain important in microgravity; they do not define a universal threshold for other 
materials or apparatus [10, 11].
10.2 Why there is no universal 5 cm/s or 30-40 cm/s extinction rule
The cited reports do not support a universal rule that combustion is radiatively extinguished below 5 
cm/s or blown off above 30-40 cm/s. Extinction limits depend on sample shape, polymer type, thickness, 
preheating, oxygen fraction, temperature, and flow direction. The observation of a flame below 1 cm/s 
in some cases directly cautions against generalizing that zero or low flow always extinguishes a fire.
10.3 Heat transfer into the solid
A specimen receives heat from the flame, hot gases, and possibly radiation; it conducts energy into its 
depth and toward the adjacent region of the flame front. Sample thickness changes thermal storage 
and conduction resistance. A thick or preheated specimen can have a different surface temperature 
and volatile-fuel release rate. BASS-related reports emphasize that thickness and preheating affect 
flame spread, illustrating why a flow threshold cannot be transferred without describing the sample 
and its thermal history.
The BASS/BASS-II evidence is directly relevant to questions of solid-material flammability in 
microgravity, but it is not a blanket certification for all polymers, geometries, or lunar-habitat 
conditions. The dashboard should store each result with material identity, thickness, orientation, 
sample temperature, oxygen environment, and velocity measurement location.

11. Large-scale spacecraft fires: SAFFIRE
The Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SAFFIRE) program conducted large-scale fire experiments 
in an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after it had separated from the ISS. This approach enabled tests 
at a scale and configuration that would not be appropriate inside an occupied spacecraft. The program 
provided observations of flame behavior, material burning, and spacecraft fire dynamics in a vehicle-
relevant enclosure [12, 13].
SAFFIRE I-III and later follow-on experiments form a series rather than one single test. NASA Glenn 
reported the conclusion of the long-running series in February 2024, and NASA materials identify 
SAFFIRE VI as the final demonstration. These experiments are important for understanding the 
interaction of flame, ventilation, and vehicle-scale geometry, but the setting remains an uncrewed 
cargo vehicle after departure from the station. It is not equivalent to a fire inside a crewed cabin with 
crew, active life-support systems, and operational constraints.
For data integration, SAFFIRE records should retain mission iteration, sample type, vehicle geometry, 
fan/ventilation configuration, camera view, and timing relative to separation from the ISS. Scale is a 
major axis of comparison; it should not be treated as incidental metadata.
12. SoFIE and FM²: from orbit to lunar gravity
12.1 SoFIE-GEL and SoFIE-MIST
The SoFIE investigations address material ignition, flame growth, and suppression using controlled test 
configurations. SoFIE-GEL (Growth and Extinction Limit) and SoFIE-MIST (Material Ignition and 
Suppression Test) have distinct sample forms and objectives [4, 5]. SoFIE-GEL includes a PMMA 
spherical sample configuration, while SoFIE-MIST uses a PMMA cylinder sample configuration. The 
datasets should be treated as related investigations rather than merged as if they used identical 
geometry and boundary conditions.
The value of SoFIE for the proposed atlas is its contribution to repeatable investigations of material 
ignition and extinction in reduced-buoyancy environments. Results must remain linked to specimen 
shape, sample heating, ventilation, oxygen concentration, and diagnostic endpoints. A result for a 
polymer sphere cannot automatically be applied to a flat sheet or a cylindrical specimen.
12.2 Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM²)
NASA describes FM² as a lunar-relevant material-flammability investigation. The sources reviewed for 
the original paper describe the investigation as planned, with preparatory terrestrial tests intended to 
simulate lunar gravity; they do not establish that the cited tests had already been conducted on the 
lunar surface [2, 3]. This distinction is essential. A planned experiment and a terrestrial partial-gravity 
simulation are not the same evidence as a direct lunar surface test.
The “Goldilocks” idea—that partial gravity might create flame behaviors different from both 1g and 
microgravity—is a testable research hypothesis, not a universal rule. Partial gravity modifies buoyancy 
but does not remove it, and the outcome remains coupled to pressure, oxygen fraction, imposed flow, 
sample geometry, and material properties.
13. FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI: droplets and cool flames
FLEX and FLEX-2 examine droplet combustion and flame extinguishment, including interactions 
between fuel droplets and gaseous environments. Cool-flame investigations (CFI) study low-
temperature oxidation regimes and chemical behavior that differs from conventional hot flames [14-

16]. These studies are relevant to combustion chemistry and extinction mechanisms but are not direct 
substitutes for solid-material flame-spread experiments.
13.1 Cool-flame chemistry and negative-temperature-coefficient behavior
Cool flames involve low-temperature oxidation pathways that can exhibit complex dependence on 
temperature and composition. In some regimes, the reaction rate may decrease as temperature rises 
over a limited range, a behavior associated with negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) chemistry. The 
existence and extent of cool-flame regimes depend on fuel, pressure, oxygen and inert-gas 
composition, and the test protocol. A single temperature interval should not be treated as a universal 
boundary for all fuels.
13.2 Transfer limits
Droplet flame extinction and cool-flame chemistry can inform general reaction and transport 
understanding, but the results cannot be transferred wholesale to a solid polymer fire. The 
characteristic fuel geometry, surface heat feedback, vaporization, and reaction pathways differ. The 
preliminary draft contained specific oxygen and ozone percentages that were not verified against a 
primary source for the intended claim; those values are therefore omitted as confirmed facts.
14. SAME, SAME-R, and MPASS: smoke aerosols
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) and its reflight (SAME-R, also called SAMER in its 
final report) investigated aerosol particles produced by overheated materials relevant to spacecraft. 
Tested materials included Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose lamp wick, Pyrell foam, and other 
source materials, with conditions spanning heating temperature and airflow [17, 18]. These aerosols 
are not all soot from a flaming hydrocarbon flame: overheated polymers, smoldering materials, and 
other sources may produce particles with different chemistry, morphology, and phase.
14.1 Aerosol moments and particle-size distributions
The SAME/SAME-R approach used multiple measurements or moments of the particle-size distribution. 
Combining suitable moments can support estimates such as arithmetic mean diameter, mass-weighted 
mean diameter, and, under an assumed lognormal distribution, geometric mean diameter and 
geometric standard deviation. The method depends on the validity of the distribution assumption and 
instrument detection ranges. A moment-based result should not be interpreted as a direct full 
distribution unless the source and method support that conclusion.
SAME-R included post-flight ground tests to improve dilution-ratio estimates and examine the 
lognormal-distribution assumption using additional instrumentation. Its final report described the 
method as a useful approach to characterizing the aerosols encountered in spacecraft, with results for 
five tested material classes [18].
14.2 Smoke transport and detector response
Microgravity changes smoke transport because buoyancy-driven motion is weakened and forced 
ventilation becomes more important. The time for aerosol to reach a detector can therefore depend on 
fan flow, duct geometry, source location, particle size, and particle properties. The SAME technical 
requirements document noted that prior in-flight smoke-detector response to liquid aerosol in 
microgravity was substantially reduced relative to normal gravity in the earlier CSD experiment, and 
hypothesized that extended particle growth at high concentration contributed to the difference [17]. 
This is a source-specific observation and hypothesis, not a universal detector-performance factor.

14.3 MPASS and particle diagnostics
NASA technology-transfer documentation describes MPASS as a Multi-Parameter Aerosol Scattering 
Sensor [19]. Its relevance is that a diagnostic system can provide more than one aerosol-related 
measurement. A dashboard should preserve the instrument’s documented measurands, calibration, 
and operating range. A single particle-size interval, such as 200-400 nm, should not be generalized to 
all smoke sources or all tests; distributions vary with material, heating conditions, and measurement 
method.
Dust can also produce false alarms or complicate smoke interpretation. A useful fire-safety 
information system should distinguish smoke and background dust when the data permit, but it must 
not claim discrimination where the instrument or dataset does not support it.
15. ACME and interpretation of mass-flow-controller data
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) program includes several 
combustion experiments and diagnostic approaches [22]. The PSI-159 files uploaded for this project 
contain selected raw time-series channels, MFC setpoint records, and camera metadata. The new data-
analysis appendix reports the exact sample counts, timestamp ranges, raw-column statistics, and 
setpoint values that can be verified from the uploaded files.
A controller voltage is not itself a volumetric flow rate. Converting an MFC setpoint from volts to SCCM 
or SLPM requires the specific device calibration, channel identity, gas type or gas-correction factor, 
full-scale range, reference conditions, and operating state. The SPICE final report documents an MKS 
Type 2179 controller with a 0-500 SCCM range and standard conditions of 0°C and 760 Torr for the 
SPICE apparatus [A1]. That specification is not a calibration curve for PSI-159 and must not be 
transferred to PSI-159 files without evidence.
The PSI-159 raw channel units are not defined in the uploaded files. Therefore, columns with names 
such as MFCA1StaticMixerFlow, MFCA3FuelFlow, EfieldVoltage, PMT, thermocouple, or radiometer are 
retained as source-column values unless the channel dictionary and calibration are supplied. The 
appendix does not convert these values to engineering quantities or interpret them beyond the column 
labels. This is a deliberate reproducibility constraint, not an analytical omission.
16. ISS, lunar surface, and future habitats
The ISS is a pressurized habitat with forced ventilation and a residual-acceleration environment that is 
commonly described as microgravity. The lunar surface has approximately one-sixth Earth gravity, but 
an inhabited lunar habitat would still require a pressurized internal atmosphere and engineered 
ventilation. The vacuum outside the habitat is not the environment in which an internal cabin fire 
would occur. Surface dust, temperature extremes, radiation, and external operations are additional 
system-level concerns, but they should not be confused with the internal combustion boundary 
conditions.

17. Research gaps and testable hypotheses
Several gaps remain across the reviewed literature and the data available for this project:

Limited cross-investigation harmonization of units, channel names, test identifiers, and calibration 
records.

Incomplete availability of raw image and video files in the upload set, particularly the TIFF/HOBJ 
files referenced by PSI-159 camera metadata.

Need for matched-condition comparisons among 1g, microgravity, and partial-gravity tests, 
including pressure, oxygen composition, and ventilation.

Need to connect flame behavior to aerosol generation and actual detector response, rather than 
assuming a single flame metric predicts detection performance.

Need to distinguish sample-scale fire tests from vehicle-scale fire demonstrations and from habitat-
scale engineering cases.

Need to preserve uncertainty, inconsistent metadata, and publication-version differences as first-
class records rather than silently resolving them.
The hypotheses in Section 2 can be extended with a reproducibility test: an independent analyst should 
be able to recover the same descriptive statistics and plots from the stored raw files, analysis script 
version, channel dictionary, and calibration package. The result should be “not computable” when 
required metadata are missing, rather than an inferred value.
18. Proposed innovation: Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas
The proposed Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas (LFAEA) is an interactive dashboard supported by 
traceable knowledge retrieval and an AI assistant. It links each experiment record to its source, gravity 
environment, fuel or material, airflow, oxygen and pressure conditions, geometry, instruments, 
evidence grade, uncertainty, and accessible files. It supports search and comparison while refusing to 
invent missing values or directly generalize ISS results to a lunar habitat.
18.1 Intended users and use cases

Students and researchers searching for PSI investigations relevant to a particular material, flame 
type, or diagnostic.

Fire-safety researchers comparing only experiments with sufficiently similar boundary conditions.

Project teams identifying missing metadata and prioritizing the next datasets to obtain.

Reviewers tracing an AI-generated summary back to a primary source, page, table, figure, or raw-
data column.
18.2 Core interface concepts

An investigation catalogue with filters for gravity level, material/fuel, experiment type, diagnostic, 
DOI, and evidence grade.

A comparison view that makes mismatched pressure, oxygen, geometry, or flow conditions visible 
before drawing a conclusion.

21. Uncertainty, AI risk, ethics, and safety limitations
The main risk of an AI-assisted evidence system is false confidence. A fluent summary may conceal a 
missing calibration, inconsistent identifier, incomplete upload, or incompatible boundary condition. 
The dashboard must therefore foreground provenance and data quality rather than only displaying 
polished charts. Missingness should be typed: “not measured,” “not included in the upload,” “not 
defined in metadata,” “not calibrated,” or “unreadable.” These states have different meanings and 
should not be collapsed into a blank cell.
The system should not provide procedural instructions for fighting a fire aboard a crewed spacecraft 
or recommend changes to ventilation, oxygen levels, or suppression-system operation. Those decisions 
belong to certified procedures, mission operators, and the vehicle’s engineered safety system. The 
research prototype is for literature navigation and scientific understanding, not live operational 
response.
Ethical and technical safeguards include clear disclosure that the project is independent and student-
developed, avoidance of NASA logos or language suggesting endorsement, respect for data licenses and 
publication rights, source attribution, version tracking, and human review of high-impact 
interpretations. Images, video, and proprietary engineering data should only be included according to 
their source permissions.

22. Conclusions
The reviewed evidence shows that microgravity and partial gravity alter the balance among buoyancy, 
forced ventilation, molecular diffusion, conduction, radiation, and chemical reaction. These changes 
affect ignition, flame spread, extinction, soot formation, and smoke-aerosol transport, but they do not 
support a single universal rule about flame shape, low-flow extinction, or particle size. The outcome 
depends on material, fuel, geometry, pressure, oxygen composition, imposed flow, thermal history, and 
diagnostic method.
NASA-STD-6001B remains an important standardized material-screening framework, while its 
specified test conditions should not be mistaken for complete coverage of all microgravity or lunar-
habitat environments. SPICE demonstrates the importance of burner diameter and coflow for smoke-
point measurements, BASS/BASS-II demonstrates material- and flow-sensitive solid combustion, 
SAFFIRE adds vehicle-scale evidence, SoFIE and FM² address material behavior in relevant reduced-
gravity settings, FLEX/CFI illuminate droplet and low-temperature chemistry, and 
SAME/SAME-R/MPASS contribute smoke-aerosol and diagnostic evidence.
The strongest project contribution is not a new universal fire threshold or an unvalidated predictor. It 
is a transparent evidence system that connects each result to its source and conditions, supports 
matched-condition comparisons, exposes uncertainty, and lets users reproduce data transformations. 
The Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas is proposed as a student prototype that can help organize the 
evidence base for future research on spacecraft and lunar-habitat fire safety.


The SPICE post-flight report lists 108 tests in Increment 18 and 155 additional tests in Increments 
19/20, totaling 263 test points. This is a different count from the 52 smoke-point outcomes.

PSI-159 A4 contains 7,749 numeric samples over 61.985 s; B1 contains 9,627 samples over 76.996 s.

1. SPICE: cross-check of final report, post-flight report, and Dotson 
thesis
The SPICE experiment studied smoke points in non-buoyant laminar round-jet diffusion flames with 
coflowing air aboard the ISS in the Microgravity Science Glovebox. The main controlled parameters 
included fuel type, burner/nozzle diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel flow. Dotson’s thesis defines the 
smoke point in terms of the observed onset of soot emission and luminous flame behavior; image 
analysis was used to support measurement of luminous flame length.

1.2 Physical trends and operational caveats
The final report and thesis discuss an empirical dependence of smoke-point luminous length on burner 
diameter and coflow velocity. The peer-reviewed study reports a fit of the form Lsp d^-0.91 ua^0.41.

It is an empirical correlation for the tested fuels, dimensions, and velocity range, not a universal 
combustion law. The thesis discusses possible residence-time and soot-oxidation interpretations but 
does not establish one universal mechanism for the trend.
The post-flight report notes that soot accumulation on the outlet screen changed the flow behavior in 
the duct. The thesis also discusses non-repeatability in some 0.41 mm propylene results across test 
days, associated with changes in outlet blockage and the fan effort needed to achieve the same air-
velocity reading. Accordingly, the state of the outlet screen is a relevant experimental condition, not 
merely a maintenance note.
The report describes typical burns of about 60 seconds and flushing the MSG volume with cabin air 
after every two burns. The crew and ground team used video to estimate smoke-point conditions, 
followed by post-flight analysis. No new video-based extraction has been performed here because the 
corresponding SPICE flight video files were not part of the uploaded set.

This note accompanies the research review “Combustion Physics, Thermodynamics, and Smoke 
Aerosols in Space Environments.” It was prepared after additional files were uploaded and updates 
specific statements in the original 14 November 2026 version. It does not replace the review body; it 
identifies newly available data and points readers to the descriptive analysis appendix.
1. What was added after the original review?

SPICE final report, post-flight report, and Dotson thesis: smoke-point counts by fuel were audited 
and compared with Increment 18 and Increments 19/20 test-point totals. Additional details on 
measurement methods, outlet-screen blockage, and repeatability were incorporated.

PSI-159 files: time-series sensor data for 21256A4 and 21256B1, three MFC setpoint files for A4, C1, 
and H5, and camera metadata for INTNS-A4 and ACME-H5 were analyzed.


Data ID 1 through 8, were examined. Numeric ranges and plots were included where the workbook 
fields supported them; conflicts were preserved rather than guessed.

Prioritized PSI combustion-file inventory: Verified, Pending, and Partial labels were reviewed to 
distinguish files actually uploaded from resources that remain outstanding.
